_comment: Franchise renames: one club that Cricsheet names two ways, and therefore holds two
This is data, not a heuristic. The candidates were produced once by
carry-over across the boundary -- and then reviewed by hand. A rule that ran on every
import would merge two real clubs the first time a coincidence cleared its threshold,
and a wrong merge is invisible: it corrupts a club's whole history and nothing fails.
Each entry names a gender explicitly. A team is (name, gender) since migration 0004,
and a rename that applies to a club's men's side need not apply to its women's.
Every entry here is one franchise slot in one competition whose name changed. The
detector also surfaces competition restructures -- England's women's regional teams
becoming county teams in 2025, the Hundred's 2025 rebrands -- which are a different
claim and are deliberately not here. See the PR body.

renames.note: WPL, the same club's women's side, renamed at the same time. 18 + 17 matches.

IPL, 2013. New owner and a new squad rather than a rebrand, so this is an assumption and not a fact: open decision 3 in the identity checklist chose to merge, because the alternative is a judgement about corporate continuity the data cannot settle.
Indian domestic; the same side under a fuller name.
Nepal Premier League; a spelling change, not a new club.
England women's: the Super League side became the regional side of the same name and geography in 2020.
IPL: the same franchise across its only two seasons, 14 matches in 2016 and 16 in 2017, having dropped the plural. Like Kathmandu Gurkhas, a spelling change rather than a new club.
